faq.a: If the cyst is ≥5 cm and complex, if torsion is suspected, or if there are signs of malignancy.
Rarely; most malignant ovarian tumors are solid or complex from the start, especially in post‑menopausal women.
faq.q: Can a simple cyst become malignant?

faq.a: Perform a thorough pelvic exam, assess size and tenderness, and arrange urgent referral if red‑flag symptoms are present.
faq.q: What is the first step if ultrasound is not available?

exam: A 22‑year‑old presents with sudden right‑sided pelvic pain and nausea – what is your immediate management? — Assess for torsion, obtain urgent ultrasound if possible, prepare for emergency laparoscopy.

How do you differentiate a functional cyst from an endometrioma on ultrasound? — Functional cyst is anechoic, thin‑walled; endometrioma shows homogeneous low‑level internal echoes ("chocolate" appearance).

A patient with known HIV has a 7‑cm complex ovarian mass – what extra considerations affect your management? — Higher risk of opportunistic infection and malignancy; ensure CD4 count, consider broader antibiotic coverage, and expedite surgical evaluation.
Why is a combined oral contraceptive not the first choice in an acute ovarian torsion? — It does not resolve torsion and may mask symptoms; surgery is required.
What laboratory test helps rule out a gestational trophoblastic disease when an adnexal mass is found? — Serum β‑hCG; a markedly elevated level suggests trophoblastic disease.

In a low‑resource clinic without ultrasound, a 30‑year‑old has a 6‑cm painless adnexal mass – what follow‑up plan do you give? — Schedule repeat pelvic exam in 6 weeks, advise to return if pain, bleeding or rapid growth occurs, and arrange referral for imaging when feasible.
ai.subject: Obstetrics & gynaecology
ai.summary: A concise guide to diagnosing, staging and managing ovarian cysts for Year‑4 students in East African hospitals, focusing on clinical assessment and limited investigations.

b: Most cysts are <5 cm and asymptomatic
Large or complex cysts may cause pain, pressure or bleeding
sections.p: An ovarian cyst is a fluid‑filled sac arising from the ovary, detected by history, pelvic exam and, when available, ultrasound.

b: Simple cyst <5 cm – observe
Complex cyst ≥5 cm or solid areas – consider surgery
sections.p: Cysts are classified by size, morphology and risk of malignancy (simple vs complex, unilocular vs multilocular, solid components).

b: Functional cyst – most frequent in reproductive age
Endometrioma – chocolate‑coloured cyst, often painful
Tubal‑ovarian abscess – PID background, febrile
Schistosomal cyst – rare, history of freshwater exposure
sections.p: In low‑resource settings the common aetiologies are functional (follicular, corpus luteum), endometriotic, tubal‑ovarian abscess and parasitic (schistosomiasis).

b: Sudden, severe unilateral pain → torsion
Gradual bloating, pressure on bladder → large cyst
Irregular bleeding → hormonal disturbance
sections.p: Patients may present with pelvic or lower‑abdominal pain, menstrual irregularities, a palpable adnexal mass, or acute abdomen if rupture or torsion occurs.

t.b: Confirms presence of an adnexal mass and assesses tenderness, mobility and size – guides urgency
Answers whether the cyst is simple or complex, its dimensions and vascular flow – determines need for surgery
Excludes pregnancy or gestational trophoblastic disease when a cyst is seen – a positive test redirects management
Detects anemia from chronic bleeding or leukocytosis in infection – supports diagnosis of tubo‑ovarian abscess

t.a: If ultrasound unavailable, diagnostic paracentesis (rare) or clinical monitoring
t.b: Provides limited information; rely on serial exams and symptom change

b: Sudden severe pain → torsion
Rapid abdominal distension, fever → rupture or abscess
Persistent vomiting, shock signs → intra‑abdominal bleeding
Suspicion of malignancy (solid areas, papillary projections) → urgent oncology referral
sections.p: Identify features that demand urgent referral or surgery.

b: Observation for simple cyst <5 cm – repeat exam in 6‑8 weeks
Analgesia (paracetamol, NSAID if no renal/bleeding risk)
Antibiotics (e.g., ampicillin‑cloxacillin) for tubo‑ovarian abscess
Surgical removal (cystectomy or oophorectomy) for torsion, large complex cysts, or suspected cancer
Avoid hormonal contraceptives that may mask torsion symptoms
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, relieve symptoms and prevent complications.

b: Repeat ultrasound after 6 weeks if cyst persisted
Educate on menstrual tracking and early reporting of pelvic pain
Treat sexually transmitted infections promptly to reduce PID‑related cysts
Consider hormonal regulation (combined oral contraceptive) after acute phase if no contraindication
sections.p: Regular review ensures resolution and detects recurrence.

b: Uterine fibroid – firm, midline mass, not adnexal
Hydrosalpinx – tubular, sausage‑shaped, often bilateral
Appendiceal mass – right lower quadrant, tenderness on McBurney’s point
sections.p: Conditions that mimic ovarian cysts on exam or imaging.

b: Simple cyst may appear complex on low‑resolution ultrasound – correlate clinically
β‑hCG false‑negative early pregnancy – repeat if suspicion remains
Leukocytosis may be absent in early tubo‑ovarian abscess – rely on pain pattern
sections.p: Pitfalls in interpretation of limited investigations.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly enlarging mass or suspicion of malignancy
